In the early eighteen hundreds, hoists already lifted goods in factories, warehouses and mines, hanging from a single rope.
If that rope broke, the platform simply dropped.

In eighteen fifty-two, a mechanic named Elisha Otis worked out a fix.
He fixed a curved steel spring, like the ones on a wagon, to the top of the platform, and tied the rope to the middle of it.
While the rope is holding the weight, it pulls the spring into a bow.
The guide rails on each side got teeth, like a ratchet.
If the rope breaks, the spring springs flat.
Its ends shoot out into the teeth, and the platform locks in place.
And here's the clever part.
Nobody has to notice anything.
The broken rope itself is the trigger.
Engineers call that fail-safe.
In eighteen fifty-four, at the Crystal Palace exhibition in New York, Otis rode his platform high above the crowd.

A modern traction elevator doesn't hang from one rope.

A thin rope loops from the car, up around a wheel called the governor, and back down.
As the car moves, the governor spins.
If it spins too fast, weights inside swing outward, and trip a clamp that grabs the governor rope.
That yanks a lever on the car, which jams steel wedges against the guide rails.
